fyp.title: Reaction Training Game Console
fyp.subtitle: -- A Cognitive Rehabilitation Device for the Elderly --

s1.title: Why This Project?
s1.p1: With the global aging population, cognitive decline and slower reaction times have become serious challenges. According to WHO (2025), the number of people over 60 will double in the coming years, and falls are a leading cause of injury among the elderly, with high medical costs. Traditional rehabilitation methods are often repetitive, boring, or purely touchscreen-based, lacking interactivity and real-time feedback, making it difficult to sustain patient engagement.
s1.p2: So we set out to build a dedicated reaction training console tailored for seniors. By combining physical buttons, an intuitive visual interface, and cloud data tracking, we aim to make rehabilitation both engaging and measurable. The device must work offline, have ultra-low latency, be intuitive to operate, and automatically log training data.
s1.imgcaption: ▲ Elderly user operating the training console

s2.title: How We Achieved It
s2.p1: Core: ESP32 microcontroller with a 3.5-inch TFT touchscreen (ILI9341) and a 3x3 matrix keypad. We designed an ergonomic 3D-printed enclosure with large buttons (>1.2 cm diameter) and wide spacing. High-contrast UI and adjustable font sizes ensure readability for users with vision impairment.
s2.p2: A non-slip grip on the left side prevents accidental drops, and internal reinforcements prevent deformation from repeated pressing.
s2.p3: We used FreeRTOS on the ESP32 to handle multi-tasking (input scanning, game logic, UI rendering), keeping button latency below 100ms. Two games are included: a Memory Game (repeat a sequence of lit buttons) and a Counting Game (count shapes and press the corresponding number). Difficulty levels: Easy, Hard, and Auto (dynamically adjusts to performance).
s2.p4: All game data (score, reaction time, mode) is stored locally in NVS and automatically syncs to Firebase Realtime Database when Wi-Fi is available.
s2.p5: We built a Web Dashboard (React + Chart.js) to visualize training records. Caregivers can view total sessions, highest scores, performance trends, and generate PDF reports. A nursing log is also included for recording observations and suggestions.
s2.imgcaption2: ▲ Dashboard showing record list and trend chart

s3.title: Testing & Results
s3.p1: We conducted thorough unit and system integration tests covering key response, offline storage, Wi-Fi connectivity, and cloud sync. Results show:
s3.li2: ✅ Offline data is fully preserved and automatically uploaded when reconnected
s3.li3: ✅ High-contrast mode and large font switch seamlessly
s3.li4: ✅ Dashboard reflects latest records in real-time

s4.title: Technical Challenges & Solutions
s4.p1: Initial attempts with LVGL and TFT_eSPI failed, causing a white screen. We switched to Adafruit_GFX + Adafruit_ILI9341 and adjusted SPI pins (CS=5, DC=17, RST=16) based on open-source references. We also fixed a deadlock issue caused by FreeRTOS mutex.
s4.p2: In the Memory Game, displaying a sequence required delays. Using `delay()` blocked button scanning. We implemented non-blocking timing with `millis()`, allowing users to interrupt or exit at any time.
s4.p3: ESP32's Preferences library doesn't support struct storage. We serialized game records into a 17-byte buffer, stored via `putBytes()`, and deserialized on boot, ensuring no data loss during prolonged offline use.

s5.title: Future Scope
s5.li1: Global leaderboard and social features (via Firebase extension)
s5.li4: Machine learning model for personalized difficulty prediction
